summary: Welcome to the Mars Navigator that will help any astronaut that has a mission on Mars, in particular, in the Acidalia Planitia region. For the NASA's Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, we have designed an interactive map, that will be able to generate the most efficient route by scanning the surroundings. To achieve this it will use the already existing maps (topographic, spectral and geophysical), cameras (stereoscopic and optical) and sensors (LiDAR) that will read and analyse points of interest around the astronaut. By triangulation,  it will calculate the astronaut's location while the mission is on board, ensuring the safety of the explorer at all times.
details:
MAЯPS: Mars Astronaut Route & Planning Simulation

Our proposal to the challenge evaluates the following points:

The real-time location method designed to operate on Mars works by overlaying three distinct layers of real-time environmental information obtained by three different sensors.  

The first step in this capture phase is to gather information simultaneously from three sources: standard visual images and color from a camera, thermal readings and different spectra sensors like heat through infrared, and terrain depth measurements captured by stereoscopic cameras to create a 3D relief.  

Then, before anything else, a quality check is performed to verify that all the captured images are sharp and valuable enough for further processing. If any of the visual, infrared or depth data turns out to be deficient, the system keeps trying to capture the images until optimal quality is achieved. 

Once the quality check is passed, all three of the validated images are fused into one single unified view of the surroundings. This view is then compared against a preloaded map to determine the concrete location of the astronaut. Finally, this position is updated in real time, and the procedure is repeated once every cycle, with each cycle lasting 30 seconds, allowing the system to recalibrate and adjust the astronaut location with greater precision every cycle whenever possible. 

  • 1. Landing zone.

A spacecraft's landing has a significant margin of error on long-range missions; therefore, prior to any analysis or scanning of any certain position, we would determine which region of Acidalia it would be landing.

  • 2. The spacecraft uses LiDAR to pinpoint its position.

The spacecraft would have an integrated system called LiDAR. Very similar to radar or sonar, this system consists of a sensor that fires laser pulses toward the surrounding surface. As the light bounces off the Martian surface and returns to the sensor, it measures the exact time each pulse took to travel back and forth.  

Knowing the speed of light and the round-trip time, a computer calculates the exact distance of each point, and by combining all these points, a 3D model called “point cloud” is generated.

By comparing this point cloud with the previously downloaded 3D map made by a big number of satellites, we can determine our exact location by matching significant features or points of interest already marked on the map. 

  • 3. Log the position (latitude, longitude, altitude) on an interactive map (automatic).

The already pinpointed position would transform in a coordinates system, matching the databases we have of mars and converting the point cloud, once aligned with the 3D map, into known coordinates on the Martian surface using the latitude and longitude system, followed by a final altitude reading for greater accuracy relative to Mars' zero-elevation point. All of this would automatically be calculated and integrated in the system and the application for faster preparation and execution of the mission and the exploration part.  

  • 4. Select the destination point.

The interactive map is a pre-loaded map of mars scanned and captured through satellites with various points of interest previously obtained and marked from official NASA data.

The astronaut uses this interface to easily select the destination from these options, also being capable at the same time being able to see the other points of interest near him in case some extra exploration needs to be made. 

  • 5. Define a safe route based on hazard points (length and travel time).

The interactive map integrates environmental and radiation risk zones derived from official NASA data. This enables the system to map hazardous areas across the Martian surface of the Acidalia Planitia. By combining these radiation risk indicators with topographical data and known obstacles like potentially dangerous craters and crevasses made by marsquakes, the software establishes the safest and most efficient route. In addition, it provides an initial estimate of both the total route distance and the expected travel duration. 

  • 6. Recalculate the route based on forecasts and new data (e.g., weather, daytime) and on newly detected hazards (stereoscopic cameras).

During the expedition, the system continuously monitors the surroundings in real time, using the wide-angle stereoscopic with an infrared-light camera included and an optic camera in the spacesuit’s helmet.

The stereoscopic camera uses a dual lens to capture simultaneous images from two slightly different perspectives. Through geometric triangulation and the calculation of disparity between both views, the system processes the information in real time to measure the exact distance to objects and accurately calculate the depth of the environment in three dimensions.  Then all of this information is shown in a HMD (Head Mounted Display), helping in the guide of the path by visualizing the terrain and the information displayed at the same time without having to look in the interactive map.

This allows for instant detection of new obstacles or unforeseen hazards. Taking these findings into account, along with forecasts and new environmental data (such as weather changes, dust storms or the available daylight window), the software dynamically recalculates the route.

Thus, the initial route adapts flexibly to the actual conditions of the area explored to always ensure the astronaut’s safety, one of the most important life of all missions.

  • 7. Save the real data obtained by the stereoscopic cameras and overwrite the obsolete data.

All the information gathered in the expedition thanks to the stereoscopic and optic camera is automatically integrated into the interactive map, overwriting the obsolete data. In this way, it is constantly updated as new data from the Martian surface is discovered and recorded. 

It also saves the astronaut’s path in case he gets lost and the app doesn’t work or fails, so he can return to the initial point. 

  • 8. Potential Backup: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU)  

As an additional safety measure against potential visibility problems or camera failures (such as severe dust storms or the temporary loss of visual references), the system could incorporate an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). This device is a microchip with accelerometers and gyroscopes that continuously measure the astronaut’s linear acceleration, angular velocity, and orientation in real time, without having to look outside.  

With the IMU, the system could estimate the astronaut’s location from the last known reliable position, even when the cameras lose visual reference, keeping the route on track and ensuring safety. 

MAЯPS BUSINESS MODEL      

Our market strategy is based on collaborating with future human space explorations on Mars. We aim to commercialize our navigation software to space agencies like NASA and private aerospace companies such as SpaceX that are already preparing these types of missions.  

In our proposed solution to the NASA Space Apps Challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, the astronaut safety and efficient route planning are essential. Therefore, we provide the critical software and hardware integration needed to help astronauts navigate and return to base safely.

WEB PAGE AND SIMULATION TUTORIAL

Next, a simple tutorial for the created web page demo, that simulates the astronaut's mission and details proposed as a solution to the challenge.  

Upon opening the application, a home page appears in the "Mission View" section, inviting the user to start a new mission.

Before starting, it is helpful to understand the sections that make up the platform. On the left, there is a menu with five sections. First, there is the "Mission View", which is already shown, where the ongoing mission is displayed step-by-step.

This is followed by "Map," which includes the map of Mars with marked points of interest, built from official NASA maps and data. The tab at the top right corner allows the user to choose between two maps: geological or satellite.

Next is "Mission Log", where the onboard mission data is accumulated, and "Mission Archive", which saves the history of the completed mission (such as the path followed) and allows exporting this data for future missions and analysis.

Finally, in this menu there is the "Mission Setup", which includes all the simulation details, such as the time multiplier, elevation data, or the region being explored. 

With everything clear and understood, the user can begin the mission in the "Mission View" section clicking the "Start mission" button, which will take you to the "Mission Setup" section to enter a custom name.

The map of Mars then appears, where the landing point must be selected, but only within the Acidalia Planitia region, as it is the area of study. The icons for each point vary in shape depending on what they represent (for example, the points where a rover has landed are star-shaped). 

Once the landing point is selected, the area data can be observed (altitude, latitude, longitude...), as well as the safety measured based on the radiation and proximity to craters. In addition, it shows the most important factors for a safe exploration, such as the slope or the nearest obstacle.

After selecting and confirming the landing point, the user has to wait for the spacecraft to land:

With the spacecraft landed, the user has to press the button to start the exploration.

Then, the platform offers a 360 degree visual image of the surroundings. Within this same interface, it is possible to select the desired destination. 

The screen displays the following in real time: at the top, the astronaut's current location and status, the external environmental conditions, the battery level of the vehicle they are traveling in, and their current distance from the landed spacecraft. At the bottom, the destination options (to select destination or return to vehicle), the navigation details (that appear after the destination is selected) and, for ease of use of the simulation, all the controls displayed at the bottom right corner.

In this way, the astronaut receives at a single glance all the necessary information to stay safe during the mission. 

To select the destination the user has to press the button "Destination" and choose between the multiples landmarks.

To reach that destination, the user must align the directional arrow with the destination marker, so that the blue diamond in the compass located at the top is centered. To ease the astronaut experience, the next movement is written below the directional arrow (e.g., Turn left 47°).

This time, the navigation details show the exploration time and distance as well as other alternatives appear in the screen.

When the arrow and the marker are aligned, the text below the arrow reads: "Straight ahead".

While the explore simulation is performed, the "Mission Log" shows the occurred events for later archiving in the "Mission Archive" section.

When the mission is over, the recorded data can be accessed using the archive.

Finally, if the user clicks on the "View" button of the mission of their choice, they will see all the data from that mission's log, accompanied by the path followed by the astronaut.
